title: Vision 1.1: Rhoda in the sky (the Visions: why repentance is needed)
sum: The book begins like a memoir. Hermas, raised as a slave and sold to a woman named Rhoda in Rome, meets her again years later, helps her out of the Tiber, and thinks: 'I would be a happy man if I had a wife like her.' Some time later, on the road to Cumae, a spirit carries him off; he kneels to confess his sins, the sky opens, and Rhoda speaks from heaven. She has been taken up to report his sin to the Lord.

Hermas protests that he never said a shameful word to her. She laughs: the evil desire rose up in his heart, and for a righteous man that is a great sin. The chapter ends with a warning to the rich who swagger in their wealth, and a promise: pray, and God will heal your sins and your household's.

This is the first of the Visions (chapters 1-25), the part of the book that, in Lake's words, enforces 'the necessity for repentance'. For all of Visions 1-4 Lake has two Greek witnesses, Codex Sinaiticus (300s) and the Athos manuscript (1400s); Sinaiticus stops at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6), after which the Athos manuscript is, in Lake's words, 'the only continuous Greek text' for most of the book.

views.H: The opening gives the first facts Hermas tells about himself: a former slave (1:1), in Rome; the Visions add a wife, children and a business (6:3; 7:1) and past riches (14:7). Lake takes the Muratorian list's date, written while Pius led the Roman church, about 148, but reports that 'many critics' think the book grew over twenty or thirty years before that. Whether the Rhoda story is memory or literary frame cannot be settled.
views.N: Rhoda's charge stands beside Jesus' teaching that desire in the heart is already sin (Matthew 5:28). The rich 'who make this world their own' recall the warnings of 1 Timothy 6:17 and James 5:1-6.
views.J: The vision follows the shape of Jewish apocalypses: a journey 'through a place with no road', prayer and confession, heaven opened, a heavenly figure who speaks. The creation from nothing (1:6) is the language of 2 Maccabees 7:28.
views.R: Everything is Roman: a household slave sold and later met again, a bath in the Tiber, the road to Cumae. A Roman reader would know the place and the social world at once.

echoes: Matthew 5:28; Ezekiel 1:1; Ezekiel 3:12; Revelation 4:1; 2 Maccabees 7:28; Romans 4:17; Genesis 1:28; 1 Timothy 6:17; Jeremiah 3:22

settings.what: Rhoda's accusation from heaven
settings.by: Rhoda, Hermas's former owner, speaking from the opened sky
settings.to: Hermas, kneeling in prayer in the countryside
settings.when: On a walk toward Cumae, some time after Hermas had seen her in the Tiber
settings.why: To show Hermas, and through him the reader, that sin begins in the heart, so that even a believer who thinks himself righteous needs repentance; and to promise that God will heal those who pray.
settings.readers: The believers in Rome who would hear the book read 'in this city with the elders who lead the church' (8:3). The scene speaks to people who, like Hermas, thought a sin that stayed in the heart did not count.

title: Vision 1.2: The old woman with the book
sum: The heavens shut, and Hermas is left shaking. If even this sin is written down against him, how can he be saved? While he turns it over, a great white chair of snow-white wool appears, and an old woman in shining clothes sits in it holding a book. She greets him, notices that the usually cheerful Hermas looks gloomy, and hears his story.

Her verdict is gentle but firm. Such a thought should never rise in a slave of God, above all in one known for self-control, simplicity and innocence; for a spirit already tested, even an evil plan in the heart brings sin. The reader does not yet know who she is. That is told in 8:1.

views.H: The old woman is not named until 8:1, and Hermas's guess there (the Sibyl) shows how a Roman would first read the figure. The scene's details, a teacher's chair and a book, are those of a woman who teaches.
views.N: The white wool recalls Daniel 7:9 and Revelation 1:14; the book in the hand recalls the scroll of Revelation 5 and 10.
views.D: The old woman's words assume a church of baptized believers held to a high standard: Lake's introduction says Hermas's circle believed 'Christians after baptism were capable of leading sinless lives'. The whole book works out what happens when they fail.

echoes: Daniel 7:9; Revelation 1:14; Revelation 5:1; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12; Jude 1:1

settings.what: The old woman's first words
settings.by: An old woman in shining clothes, later revealed as the Church (8:1)
settings.to: Hermas, alone and grieving after Rhoda's vision
settings.when: Immediately after the first vision closes
settings.why: To comfort Hermas without excusing him: she confirms that the thought was sin for a tested believer, and prepares him to hear that God's anger has another cause (3:1).
settings.readers: Believers in Rome who, like Hermas, thought themselves upright and needed to hear that sin begins with the will.

title: Vision 1.3: Hermas's household and the reading
sum: Now the old woman gives the real reason for God's anger: not Hermas's thought, but his household. His children have broken the law against the Lord and their parents, and he, loving them too much, never corrected them. He has been ruined by everyday business. But the Lord's compassion has had mercy on them all. If Hermas keeps correcting them with a daily righteous word, as a smith hammers his work into shape, and if they repent with all their heart, they will be written in the books of life.

Then she reads from her book. Most of it is too terrifying to remember, but Hermas keeps the gentle ending, a hymn: God made the world by power and wisdom, founded the earth on the waters, created his holy church, and now moves the heavens and mountains to make a level road for his chosen, if they keep his rules.

views.H: The Amherst papyrus, an early papyrus copy, covers part of these chapters, and its reading at 3:1 agrees with Sinaiticus against the Athos manuscript (see the variant). Lake marks 3:4 as 'clearly corrupt'.
views.N: Hermas's failure as a father is Eli's (1 Samuel 3:13) and the opposite of the overseer of 1 Timothy 3:4-5, who keeps his children in order. The hymn echoes the creation psalms (Psalm 24:2; Psalm 136:6).
views.R: The book shows Hermas as a man of business, 'tangled up' in his dealings (7:1), who had once been rich (14:7); here those dealings are what ruined him (3:1).

echoes: 1 Samuel 3:13; 1 Timothy 3:4-5; Titus 2:4; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; Psalm 24:2; Psalm 136:6; Isaiah 40:4; 2 Corinthians 12:4

settings.what: The old woman's word on Hermas's household
settings.to: Hermas, a father whose children have gone wrong
settings.when: Still in the first vision
settings.why: To turn Hermas from self-reproach over one thought to his real duty: correcting his family, and to give him hope that they can still repent.
settings.readers: Christian households in Rome; the book later sends Hermas's message to his children and wife by name (6:3), and through the book to every family in the church.

settings.what: The reading from the book (a hymn of creation)
settings.to: Hermas, listening
settings.when: At the end of the first vision
settings.why: To set the call to repent inside God's whole plan: the God who made the world and the church will make the road level for his chosen if they keep faith.
settings.readers: The congregation that would hear the book read aloud with the elders (8:3). The hymn gives them the gentle words that are 'for the righteous' (4:2), after the hard ones they are spared.

title: Vision 1.4: The chair carried east
sum: The reading ends, and four young men carry the chair away toward the east. The old woman touches Hermas's chest and asks if he liked her reading. He liked the ending; the beginning was harsh. She explains: the last words are for the righteous, the first for the nations and the deserters. Two men lead her away toward the east, and she leaves cheerful, calling, 'Be brave, Hermas!'

views.N: The split between words for the righteous and words for those outside (4:2) is the split of Jesus' parables explained to the disciples and kept in riddles for outsiders (Mark 4:11-12), though Hermas's point is about judgment and mercy.
views.D: 'The nations' here are the unbaptized (compare 6:5). The book's message of a second chance is aimed at baptized believers; for those outside, the usual call to repent and be baptized stands.

echoes: Genesis 2:8; Ezekiel 43:2; Mark 4:11-12; 1 Corinthians 16:13; Joshua 1:6

settings.what: The old woman's farewell
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: As the first vision ends
settings.why: To leave Hermas with courage, not terror: the hard words are for others; for the righteous, the message is hope.
settings.readers: Believers in Rome, who would hear that the harsh words were for 'the nations' and the deserters (4:2) and that the parting word was courage.

title: Vision 2.1: The little book copied (Vision 2: the one chance to repent)
sum: A year later, at the same season and on the same road, the spirit carries Hermas to the same place. He prays and thanks God for showing him his sins. The old woman appears again, walking and reading a little book, and asks if he can announce its words to God's chosen. He cannot remember so much, so she lends it to him. He copies it letter by letter, unable to tell where the syllables break, and the moment he finishes, it is snatched from his hand.
Vision 2 (chapters 5-8) is the message of the little book: forgiveness for past sins, one more time, with a deadline.

views.H: Lake explains the copying: the book was written 'like most early MSS., in a continuous script with no divisions between the words'. The scene shows a book copied by hand, and 8:3 shows the next step: two copies made and sent out.
views.N: The little book is the word of Revelation 10:2, 9-10, where John is given a little scroll. Prophets receive written words from heaven in Ezekiel 2:9-3:3.
views.R: Cumae, if that is the place (see the variant at 1:3), lay on the coast west of Naples, a long way from Rome; the trip at 'the same season' every year may be a summer visit to the country.

echoes: Revelation 10:2; Revelation 10:9-10; Ezekiel 2:9-10; Ezekiel 3:1-3

settings.what: The old woman's commission
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: A year after the first vision, on the same road
settings.why: To make Hermas a messenger: what he receives is for 'God's chosen', not for himself alone.
settings.readers: God's chosen in Rome, to whom Hermas was to announce the book (5:3), and through Clement's copy the churches abroad (8:3).

title: Vision 2.2: The one chance to repent
sum: After fifteen days of fasting and prayer, Hermas understands what he copied. It is a message for his family and for the whole church. His children have rejected God, blasphemed and betrayed their parents; his wife does not hold her tongue. But once they hear these words, all their past sins will be forgiven, and so will the sins of all the saints up to this day, if they repent with all their heart.

Then the deadline. God has sworn by his own glory: if anyone sins again now that this day has been set, there is no salvation for him. 'The days of repentance are over for all the saints', though for 'the nations' repentance stays open until the last day. The leaders must set their ways straight; those who endure the great suffering that is coming are blessed; those who deny 'their Christ' in the days ahead are cut off, while those who denied before are forgiven.
readings: Read on its own terms, 6:4-5 announces a single, dated offer: everything up to 'this day' is forgiven to the baptized who repent, and after it there is no more. The deadline is the point, and the rest of the book (Mandate 4, 31) defends it: 'one repentance'.

Lake's reading: the 'primitive teaching' allowed no repentance after baptism (he points to Hebrews 6), and Hermas's revelation opens the door once more. On this view the deadline is Hermas's way of making the offer acceptable to strict believers: not a new rule that sin is easy to forgive, but one exceptional grace.

The deadline also stands beside the coming 'great suffering' (6:7) and the tower's completion (13:5; 16:9). On this reading the urgency is about the end: repent now, because time is short, as in 2 Peter 3:9.

views.H: Lake's footnote calls 6:5 'the main point of the Shepherd'. The verses also show the church's leaders addressed as a group (6:6) and a recent or coming persecution in which some denied Christ (6:7-8; 7:4).
views.N: Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is 'impossible' to bring back to repentance those who once received the light and fell away; Hebrews 10:26 says no sacrifice for sins is left for those who keep on sinning by choice. Hermas both agrees (no endless repentance) and differs (one more chance now). God's oath (6:5) is the language of Hebrews 6:13-18.
views.D: The chapter is the starting point of a long debate in the churches: can serious sin after baptism be forgiven, and how often? See the deep section below, and the chapter page of 31 (Mandate 4.3).
views.R: Denial in persecution (6:8; 7:4) fits a city where Christians could be brought before Roman magistrates and asked to deny the Name.

deep.h: Repentance after baptism: what Hermas says
deep.b: Three things are said here and must be kept together. First, forgiveness is real and wide: all the sins of Hermas's family, and 'of all the saints who have sinned up to this day', are forgiven if they repent with all their heart and drive out double-mindedness (6:4). Second, it has a limit: God has sworn that 'if anyone sins any more now that this day has been set, he will not be saved', for 'repentance for the righteous has an end' (6:5). Third, the limit is for the baptized only: 'for the nations there is repentance until the last day'. Vision 3 restates the deadline as the finishing of the tower (13:5), and Mandate 4 gives the rule in its best-known form: after the great and holy calling, 'one repentance' (31:6). Lake's judgment, from his introduction: 'the message of Hermas was that for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once', and 'we have here the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance'. That is Lake's view; readers in other churches weigh it differently.

deep.h: How the early church read it
deep.b: Clement of Alexandria teaches close to Hermas: 'He, then, who has received the forgiveness of sins ought to sin no more', and he speaks of a repentance for those who fall after their calling beside 'the first and only repentance from sins' (Stromata 2.13, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation). Tertullian, in On Modesty, attacked a bishop who forgave adultery after baptism and attacked the Shepherd with him: 'the scripture of the Shepherd, which is the only one which favours adulterers', which 'every council of Churches (even of your own)' had judged 'among apocryphal and false (writings)', and he mocks 'the ewe of (your) second repentance' (On Modesty 10). So by Tertullian's time the Shepherd was a byword for a merciful second repentance, valued by some and scorned by others. In Rome in 251 Novatian set himself up as a rival bishop to Cornelius and held that idolatry was an unpardonable sin and that the church had no right to restore to communion those who had fallen into it; penitents could be admitted to lifelong penance, but their forgiveness was left to God (John Chapman in the Catholic Encyclopedia). The dispute over how far the door stands open after baptism runs from Hebrews through Hermas to these quarrels.

Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is 'impossible' to renew to repentance those who have fallen away after tasting the heavenly gift. Hermas does not quote Hebrews, but Lake reads 6:5 against it ('cf. Heb. vi.'), and the stones 'that have turned away from the living God for good' (15:2) stand where Hebrews' apostates stand: the problem is a heart in which repentance no longer rises. The site's notes on Hebrews 6 give the readings of that passage; the chapter page of 31 (Mandate 4.3) gives the churches' answers to the question Hermas raises.

echoes: Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; Hebrews 6:13-18; James 1:12; Revelation 7:14; Matthew 10:33; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Corinthians 7:5; 2 Peter 3:9

settings.what: The message of the little book
settings.by: The old woman's book, revealed to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, his children and his wife (6:3), the church's leaders (6:6), and all 'the saints'
settings.when: Fifteen days after he copied it, after fasting and prayer (6:1)
settings.why: To announce one more chance of forgiveness for baptized believers who had sinned, with a fixed deadline, and to prepare them for a coming persecution in which they must not deny Christ.
settings.readers: The Roman church, for whom the book was copied (8:3), including people like Maximus who had denied the faith once before (7:4).
views: The 'main point of the Shepherd': a new offer of forgiveness for sin after baptism, made once.
The urgency comes from the expected end and persecution, as 6:7 and 13:5 suggest.

title: Vision 2.3: Grudges, simplicity, and a word for Maximus
sum: The book's message turns to Hermas himself. He must stop holding a grudge against his children and must not neglect his wife, now his 'sister', so they may be cleansed; grudges bring death. His own troubles came from neglecting his family and getting tangled in his business. What saves him is that he never turned away from the living God, and his simplicity and self-control. 'Blessed are all who do what is right.'

Then a sharp word for one Maximus, whose 'deny again' implies he had denied before: 'Look, suffering is coming. If you think it best, deny again.' And a quotation, the only written source Hermas names: 'The Lord is near to those who turn back', from the lost Book of Eldad and Modad (the Greek spells the second name Modat).

views.J: The book of Eldad and Modad was named after the two men who prophesied in Israel's camp (Numbers 11:26-29). Lake notes it was listed among the apocrypha by the Stichometry of Nicephorus and the Synopsis of pseudo-Athanasius but is lost. That a Roman Christian quotes it with 'as it is written' shows a book outside the Hebrew Bible, named for two prophets of Israel, being read in his church.
views.N: 'Not turning away from the living God' is the language of Hebrews 3:12, and 'Blessed are all who do what is right' echoes the Psalms (Psalm 106:3; Psalm 15:2).
views.D: The quotation is about turning back (epistrephomenois), the hope held out even to a man who denied: the Shepherd's message is that God is near to those who return.

echoes: Hebrews 3:12; Psalm 106:3; Psalm 15:2; Numbers 11:26-29; Psalm 145:18; Psalm 34:18; 2 Clement 11:2; Matthew 6:14-15

settings.what: A message for Maximus
settings.to: Maximus, a member of Hermas's church whose 'deny again' implies he had denied before
settings.when: With a persecution expected soon
settings.why: To confront Maximus with the coming suffering ('If you think it best, deny again', which can be read as irony) and to hold out the promise that the Lord is near to those who turn back.
settings.readers: Maximus himself, and every Roman believer who had denied Christ under pressure and wondered whether there was a way back.

title: Vision 2.4: The Church, old because created first
sum: An angel in the form of a handsome young man asks Hermas who he thinks the old woman is. 'The Sibyl,' says Hermas. 'You are wrong. She is the Church.' Why is she old? 'Because she was created first of all. That is why she is old. And the world was put in order for her sake.'

In a later vision at home the old woman asks if Hermas has given the book to the elders yet. He has not, which is well: she has more to add. When it is finished, he is to make two copies, one for Clement, who will send it to the cities abroad, and one for Grapte, who will instruct the widows and orphans. Hermas himself will read it in Rome with the elders who lead the church.

views.H: 8:3 is the key verse for the book's date. If Clement is the writer of 1 Clement, the Visions are early; but Lake judges that 'Hermas is probably somewhat later than I. Clement, and the reference may be merely a literary device'. The verse also shows how a Roman Christian book was published: copied, read to the church by its author with the elders, and sent abroad by the church's letter-writer.
views.N: The Church before creation is close to Ephesians 1:4 ('he chose us in Christ before the world was founded') and Galatians 4:26 ('the Jerusalem above ... is our mother'). The church's elders who 'lead' use the verb of 1 Timothy 5:17.
views.J: A heavenly figure who exists before the world recalls Jewish Wisdom, who says she was made 'at the beginning of his way' (Proverbs 8:22-23).
views.D: 8:3 shows how one Roman book pictured its church: elders in the plural, a Clement with a task, a woman with another, and no single overseer named. The site's cards on bishops and elders (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1) give the churches' views; Hermas only shows what one Roman book assumed.
views.R: Hermas met the old woman with a book on the road to Cumae, the seat of the Cumaean Sibyl, whose Sibylline Books Rome kept on the Capitoline for emergencies. A Roman reader would make the same guess.

deep.h: The Church as an old woman
deep.b:
Hermas's Church appears as a woman four times, and her age changes: very old and seated (Vision 1), younger in face but old in body and hair, standing (Vision 2), young and beautiful with only her hair old, seated on a couch (Vision 3), and in Vision 4 a young woman in white 'as if she were coming out of a bridal room', with white hair (23:1). Two explanations are given. Here the young man says she is old 'because she was created first of all', and the world was made for her. In 19-21 another young man explains the change of age by the state of the believers: her age mirrored 'your' weary spirit, and as they were renewed she grew young. The two are not in conflict. One is about what the Church is before God: older than creation, the purpose for which the world exists. The other is about how she appears in a church that is tired, double-minded and worn by business, and how she is renewed by repentance.

The idea of a Church made before the world is shared by 2 Clement: 'the first church, the spiritual one, which was created before the sun and moon' (2 Clement 14:1). Paul speaks of God choosing his people 'in Christ before the world was founded' (Ephesians 1:4) and of 'the Jerusalem above' as 'our mother' (Galatians 4:26). Revelation pictures God's people as a woman clothed with the sun (Revelation 12:1) and as a bride (Revelation 21:2), which Hermas's last form recalls.

Hermas's guess is natural. He met an old woman with a book of prophecy on the road to Cumae, the seat of the Cumaean Sibyl, priestess of Apollo's oracle there; in the Roman story the Sibylline Books were bought by King Tarquinius Superbus and kept in the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill, to be consulted in emergencies. Jews and Christians also wrote oracles under her name (the Sibylline Oracles). The young man's correction is short: 'You are wrong. She is not.' The figure Hermas sees looks like Rome's prophetess, but she is the Church. The book uses the pagan picture and replaces it; it does not treat the Sibyl as a source of truth.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a new book of oracles for Rome
deep.b: Rome's Sibylline Books were kept on the Capitoline and consulted in emergencies. Hermas's old woman, mistaken for the Sibyl near Cumae, also has a book, which she lends, adds to, and orders copied for the church and sent abroad. I suggest that the scene deliberately sets the Church's little book against the Sibyl's: Rome's people had their sacred oracles, and the church in Rome now had its own, given by the Church herself, with a message of repentance before a coming crisis (6:7; 23:5). This is my reading; I have not checked whether a published study argues it.
deep.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 1:3; Shepherd of Hermas 5:3; Shepherd of Hermas 8:1-3

echoes: Ephesians 1:4; Galatians 4:26; Revelation 12:1; Revelation 21:2; 2 Clement 14:1-2; Proverbs 8:22-23; 1 Timothy 5:17; James 1:27; Philippians 4:3

settings.what: The young man's revelation about the old woman
settings.by: A very handsome young man, an angel
settings.to: Hermas, asleep
settings.when: After the second vision
settings.why: To correct Hermas's guess and give the key to all the Visions: the woman is the Church, older than the world.
settings.readers: The Roman believers who would hear the book read (8:3). Many of them would know of the Sibyl, and the young man's answer tells them whose voice the book carries.

settings.what: The old woman's orders for publishing the book
settings.to: Hermas, in his house
settings.when: When the book is to be completed
settings.why: To send the message to the whole church: abroad through Clement, to the widows and orphans through Grapte, and to the Roman congregation through Hermas reading with the elders.
settings.readers: This verse names the first readers: the church in Rome with its elders, the widows and orphans in Grapte's care, and the churches of 'the cities abroad' to which Clement wrote.

title: Vision 3.1: The couch in the field (Vision 3: the tower)
sum: After many fasts, Hermas is told to go at the fifth hour to his field in the country. He finds an ivory couch with a linen cushion and cloth, set out with no one there, and his hair stands on end. He confesses his sins again. The old woman comes with six young men, tells him to ask about righteousness and not only about his sins, and sends the young men off to build.

When Hermas tries to sit on the right side of the couch, she will not let him. The right belongs to those who have suffered for the Name; he must sit on the left. Vision 3 (chapters 9-21) is the longest of the Visions: the tower built on the water, the stones that go into it and those that do not, the seven women who hold it up, and the meaning of the Church's changing age.

views.N: The right-hand seats recall James and John's request (Matthew 20:21-23). Suffering 'for the sake of the Name' is the phrase of Acts 5:41.
views.D: The place on the right (9:9-10:1) belongs to all who bore 'whips, prisons, great sufferings, crosses, and wild beasts' for the Name; yet both sides of the couch have 'the same gifts and the same promises' (10:1).
views.R: Hermas is sent to a field in the country (9:2); the ivory couch with fine linen set out there is costly furniture.

echoes: Matthew 20:21-23; Mark 10:37-40; Acts 5:41; Job 4:15; Daniel 9:3

settings.what: The old woman's promise to appear
settings.by: The old woman, appearing at night
settings.to: Hermas, after many fasts
settings.when: Before the third vision
settings.why: To answer Hermas's prayer for the promised revelation and to set the time and place where she will show it.
settings.readers: Believers who, like Hermas, prayed and fasted to understand, and would hear that the asking was answered.

settings.what: The old woman on the seats of honor
settings.to: Hermas, at the couch in his field
settings.when: At the start of the third vision
settings.why: To teach Hermas humility and to honor the martyrs: he must not claim the place of those who suffered.
settings.readers: A church that had seen members suffer for the Name, and needed to know how to honor them without making others second-class.

title: Vision 3.2: The tower built on the water
sum: Hermas begs to see the vision, and the old woman sits him on the left. Lifting a shining staff, she shows him a great tower being built on the water from shining square stones. Six young men build it; tens of thousands of others bring stones from the deep and from the dry land. The stones from the deep fit so perfectly that the tower looks like one stone. Of those from the land, some are set in, some thrown away, some smashed and thrown far off. Many lie around the tower unused: scabby, cracked, cut short, or white and round. Others roll off the road into wild country, fall into fire, or fall near the water but cannot roll in.
readings: As the Church in the world

The tower is the Church being built now, out of believers of every kind; the unused stones are Christians who, for various faults, are not yet fit. The vision is a portrait of a real congregation in Rome.
The tower will be finished at the end (16:9), and the stones still outside then will have no place. On this reading the vision is about the final judgment of the baptized.

views.N: The tower is the 'spiritual house' of 1 Peter 2:5 and the temple 'fitted together' of Ephesians 2:20-22. Paul's builder whose work is tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:12-15) stands behind the stones that burn.
views.J: In the Animal Apocalypse of 1 Enoch a 'high tower' on God's house stands for the temple (1 Enoch 89:50); the Shepherd's tower stands for the Church. The building of God's people as a house is an old Jewish picture (Amos 9:11).
views.D: Similitude 9 (78-110) tells the tower again, with a rock and a gate (the Son of God, 89) and twelve mountains. Compared with that telling, here the emphasis is on baptism and the waters (11:5), there on Christ as the foundation.

echoes: Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5; 1 Corinthians 3:9-15; Matthew 16:18; 1 Kings 6:7; 1 Enoch 89:50; Genesis 11:4

settings.what: The old woman on the two sides of the holy place
settings.to: Hermas, upset at being sent to the left
settings.when: In the third vision, before the tower is shown
settings.why: To honor those who suffered for the Name and to tell everyone else that both sides have the same gifts and promises, and that the single-minded will be cleansed.
settings.readers: A church with members who had suffered whips, prisons and beasts for the Name, and others who had not.

title: Vision 3.3: The tower is the Church
sum: Hermas asks what it all means. The old woman calls him 'a sly man' and 'shameless', but agrees to explain: 'The tower that you see being built is I myself, the Church.' Only let his heart be toward God and not double-minded. Why is the tower built on water? 'Because your life was saved through water, and will be saved.' It is founded by the word of the almighty and glorious Name and held together by the Master's unseen power.

views.N: Life saved through water is the link 1 Peter 3:20-21 makes between the flood and baptism. 'Shameless' asking is the persistence Jesus praises in Luke 11:8.
views.D: 11:5 makes the tower stand on baptism. The churches agree that baptism belongs to entry into the Church, and differ on how it saves; see the site's cards at Acts 2, Mark 16 and Romans 6.
views.H: Clement of Alexandria quotes 11:4 ('Whatever may be revealed to you, shall be revealed') as the words of 'the power that appeared in the vision to Hermas' (Stromata 2.1).

echoes: 1 Peter 3:20-21; Titus 3:5; Luke 11:8; Ephesians 2:21; John 3:5

settings.what: The old woman's explanation of the tower
settings.to: Hermas, who is to tell 'the brothers' (11:1)
settings.when: During the third vision
settings.why: To show the church in Rome what it is and who belongs in it, so that those who hear may rejoice or weep, repent, and be built in while there is time.
settings.readers: The Roman congregation in all its variety: leaders, martyrs, new believers, the double-minded, the rich, and those who wanted baptism but drew back.

title: Vision 3.4: The six angels and the stones
sum: The six young men who build are 'the holy angels of God who were created first', to whom the Lord handed over all his creation. The others who carry stones are angels too, under the six. When the tower is finished, all will rejoice around it. Hermas asks about the stones, and is told plainly: he is not the most worthy to receive this. It is given to him for the sake of the double-minded, who doubt whether these things are true.

views.J: Jewish writings know seven chief angels (Tobit 12:15; 1 Enoch 20). Hermas's six, with countless angels under them, rule creation: a Jewish picture of angels set over the world.
views.N: Angels as builders and helpers of God's people echo Hebrews 1:14 ('spirits sent out to serve').
views.D: Lake notes that 'power' here means 'meaning' (12:3). The point for readers is assurance: 'all these things are true'.

echoes: Tobit 12:15; 1 Enoch 20:1-8; Hebrews 1:14; Revelation 8:2; James 1:6-8

title: Vision 3.5: The stones built in
sum: The square white stones that fit perfectly are 'the apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons' who lived in reverence and agreed with one another, some now asleep, some still living. The stones from the deep are those who suffered for the Lord's name. Stones from the land that go in uncut are those the Lord approved; those still being shaped are new believers. Stones set aside near the tower are sinners who want to repent: they will be used if they repent now, while the tower is being built. After that there is no place for them.

views.H: 13:1 lists 'apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons' as the stones that fit. The clause 'some of them have fallen asleep, and some are still living' covers all four groups, so the verse does not show which were dead when Hermas wrote, and it cannot date the book without a view of who 'apostles' are. Lake follows Sinaiticus at 13:4 (wickedness 'found' in the new believers); other witnesses say 'not found'.
views.N: The list joins Philippians 1:1 (overseers and deacons) and Ephesians 4:11 (apostles, teachers).
views.D: The verse does not rank the ministers or say how overseers and elders relate; see the site's cards on bishops and elders at 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1.

echoes: Philippians 1:1; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Corinthians 12:28; 1 Kings 6:7; 2 Peter 3:9

title: Vision 3.6: The rejected stones and the round stones
sum: The stones smashed and thrown far away are hypocrites, 'children of lawlessness', who have no salvation. The scabby stones knew the truth and did not stay in it. The cracked stones keep grudges and wear 'a face of peace'. The stones cut short are mostly righteous, with some lawlessness. The white round stones are believers who have faith but also 'the wealth of this world', and deny their Lord in persecution for its sake. They will be useful only when their wealth is cut away, as a round stone must be trimmed to be square. Hermas is the example: when rich, he was no use; now he is useful.

views.N: The round stones are the seed among thorns, choked by 'the trickery of wealth' (Matthew 13:22), and the rich who find it hard to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23-25).
views.R: Rome's Christians included traders and property owners. Under persecution, those with most to lose had most reason to deny.
views.D: Hermas does not say the rich must give up everything: 14:6 speaks of wealth 'cut away', and Similitude 2 (51) gives the rich a place in supporting the poor. The text leaves open whether Hermas means losing wealth by persecution or giving it up by choice.

echoes: Matthew 13:22; Mark 10:23-25; 1 Timothy 6:9-10; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; James 5:1-3

title: Vision 3.7: The stones on the road, in the fire, by the water
sum: The stones that roll off the road are the double-minded, who leave the true way for a 'better' one and wander. Those that fall into fire have turned from the living God for good: repentance no longer enters their hearts. Those that fall near the water but cannot roll in heard the message and wanted to be baptized, but drew back at the purity it demanded. Still shameless, Hermas asks whether the rejected stones have repentance. They do, but not in this tower: they will fit a much lower place, after torment that serves out the days of their sins, and only if repentance enters their hearts.

views.N: The fire recalls Hebrews 6:4-8 (land that bears thorns ends by burning) and 1 Corinthians 3:15. The ones who draw back from baptism recall the seed on rocky ground (Matthew 13:20-21).
views.D: 15:6 is an early witness to the idea of a second, lower place of salvation after a time of punishment. Lake calls the last sentence obscure and suspects words lost. For how the churches teach about cleansing after death, see the topic on purgatory.
views.H: The variant at 15:6 shows Lake keeping Sinaiticus where it 'can scarcely be quite correct' rather than accept a scribe's repair.

echoes: James 1:8; Matthew 7:13-14; Hebrews 3:12; Hebrews 6:4-8; Acts 2:38; 1 Corinthians 3:15

title: Vision 3.8: The seven women around the tower
sum: Seven women hold up the tower by the Lord's command. The first, with clasped hands, is Faith, through whom God's chosen are saved. The second, girded and strong, is Self-control, Faith's daughter. The others are Simplicity, Innocence, Reverence, Understanding and Love, each born from the one before. Whoever serves them will live in the tower with God's saints.

Hermas asks if the end has come. 'You senseless man! Don't you see that the tower is still being built?' When it is finished, the end comes, and it will be built quickly. Hermas is to wait three days to understand, and then speak it all into the ears of the saints.

views.N: The chain of virtues from Faith to Love is close to 2 Peter 1:5-7, which also runs from faith to love. The end tied to the completion of God's people recalls Revelation 6:11.
views.H: Clement of Alexandria quotes 16:3: 'The virtue, then, that encloses the Church in its grasp, as the Shepherd says, is Faith' (Stromata 2.12).
views.D: Faith comes first and Love last. How faith and works relate is read differently by the churches; see the site's cards at Romans 3 and James 2.

echoes: 2 Peter 1:5-7; 1 Corinthians 13:13; Galatians 5:22-23; Mark 13:4; Acts 1:6-7; Revelation 6:11

settings.what: The old woman on the seven women and the end
settings.to: Hermas, who is to speak it 'into the ears of the saints' (16:11)
settings.when: In the third vision, after the explanation of the stones
settings.why: To show which virtues hold the Church up and in what order they grow from Faith, and to answer the question of the end: it comes when the tower is finished.
settings.readers: Roman believers asking whether the end had come, who needed to hear that the building was still going on and what life would keep them in it.

title: Vision 3.9: The Church's charge to her children
sum: The old woman speaks to the whole church as a mother. She raised them in simplicity and innocence, but they will not stop their wickedness. They must keep the peace, care for one another, and share with those in need: some make themselves ill by eating too much while others waste away for lack of food. The rich must seek out the hungry before the tower is finished, or the needy will groan to the Lord and the rich will be shut out with their goods. To the leaders and those in the front seats she says: do not be like poisoners who carry drugs in boxes, while you carry poison in your hearts. How can you train the Lord's chosen if you have no training yourselves?

views.N: The groaning of the poor rising to the Lord is James 5:4; the front seats are those of Matthew 23:6. Sharing with those in need echoes Acts 2:44-45 and 1 Corinthians 11:21-22.
views.R: The church reproduced at its own tables a divide between those made ill by eating too much and those wasting away for lack of food (17:3).
views.D: The charge to leaders shows the church in Rome troubled by quarrels among those who led it (17:7-10).

echoes: James 5:4; Matthew 23:6; Matthew 25:35; Matthew 25:10-12; Isaiah 58:7; 1 Corinthians 11:21-22; Hebrews 13:17; Isaiah 45:8; Psalm 47:2

settings.what: The Church's charge to her children
settings.by: The old woman, the Church, speaking as a mother
settings.to: All the believers, and especially 'you who lead the church' and 'you who take the front seats' (17:7)
settings.when: At the end of her explanation in the third vision
settings.why: To call the rich to share and the leaders to make peace, before the tower is finished and it is too late.
settings.readers: A Roman congregation with rich and poor members at the same meals and leaders who quarreled for the places of honor.

title: Vision 3.10: Why the woman looked old, then young
sum: The six young men carry the old woman to the tower, and four others carry the couch. Hermas asks about the three forms she took: very old and seated last year; younger in face but old in body, standing, in the second vision; young and beautiful, with only her hair old, seated on a couch, in the third. She tells him to ask someone else. After a day's fast a young man appears and scolds him for asking so much, but Hermas presses: 'from you, sir, we will learn them more exactly.'

views.N: Fasting with humility before asking God (18:6) is the posture of Daniel 9:3 and Psalm 35:13.
views.D: The young man's warning against fasting that harms the body (18:7) shows the book's moderation: Similitude 5 (54-56) gives its teaching on a fast whose savings go to the poor.

echoes: Daniel 9:3; Daniel 10:2-3; Psalm 35:13; Matthew 6:16-18

settings.what: The old woman and the young man on Hermas's asking
settings.by: The old woman in a night vision, then a young man
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: After the third vision, before and after his one-day fast
settings.why: To teach that every request needs humility, and to check Hermas's endless asking, while still granting the explanation he presses for.
settings.readers: Believers eager for more revelations, who would hear both that they may ask and that what they have is enough (18:8).

title: Vision 3.11: The first form: an old, tired spirit
sum: The young man explains. She looked old and sat in a chair because 'your spirit is old and already withered' (the 'your' is plural, as Lake notes): weakened by double-mindedness and the business of everyday life, they had given themselves to listlessness and not thrown their worries on the Lord. Like old people who expect nothing but death, they had grown old with their griefs. She sat because the weak need a chair.

views.N: 'Throw every worry you have onto him' (1 Peter 5:7; Psalm 55:22). Renewal of the inner self day by day is Paul's theme in 2 Corinthians 4:16.
views.D: The first form is a diagnosis of a whole church, not of one man.

echoes: 1 Peter 5:7; Psalm 55:22; 2 Corinthians 4:16; Isaiah 40:30-31

settings.what: The young man's explanation of the three forms
settings.to: Hermas, speaking for 'we' (18:10), the church
settings.when: After Hermas's one-day fast at the end of the third vision
settings.why: To show the believers that the Church's look of age was their own weariness, and that the revelation has made them young again if they repent and keep the peace.
settings.readers: Roman Christians tired by long years of pressure and business, who needed to hear that they could be renewed.

title: Vision 3.12: The second form: an old man's inheritance
sum: In the second vision she stood, younger in face but old in body and hair. The young man tells a parable: an old man who has given up hope because of weakness and poverty suddenly inherits a fortune. He gets up, puts on strength, and stands. His spirit is made new. So the believers, hearing the revelation, have laid aside their weakness, and the Lord, glad at their new strength, showed them the tower, and will show more if they keep the peace with all their heart.

views.N: Renewal 'like the eagle' (Psalm 103:5; Isaiah 40:31) and an inheritance that changes everything (1 Peter 1:3-4) stand behind the parable.
views.D: The renewing is God's compassion first ('he had compassion on you') and the believers' response second: a balance the book keeps throughout.

echoes: Psalm 103:5; Isaiah 40:31; 1 Peter 1:3-4; Ephesians 4:23

title: Vision 3.13: The third form: young and joyful
sum: In the third vision she was young, lovely and cheerful. As someone in grief forgets it all at good news, so the believers have been renewed by what they have seen. She sat on a couch, a firm seat with four legs, for the world too is held together by four elements. Those who repent completely, with all their heart, will be young and firmly founded. The revelation is now complete.

views.H: Hermas takes the four elements (21:3) as common knowledge and uses them in passing.
views.N: Good news that turns grief to joy (Isaiah 61:3; John 16:20-22).
views.D: Full repentance makes the Church young: the visions end not with a threat but with a promise of renewal.

echoes: Isaiah 61:3; John 16:20-22; Wisdom of Solomon 7:17; 2 Peter 3:10

title: Vision 4.1: The beast on the road (Vision 4: the coming suffering)
sum: Twenty days later, walking into the country along the Campanian Way, Hermas asks the Lord to complete the revelations. A voice like an echo answers: 'Do not be double-minded, Hermas.' Then a cloud of dust rises to the sky. A huge beast like a sea monster comes, a hundred feet long, its head like a piece of pottery, fiery locusts coming from its mouth, rushing as if it could wreck a city. Hermas weeps, remembers the word, puts on faith, and walks toward it. The monster stretches out on the ground, puts out only its tongue, and lets him pass. On its head are four colors: black, fire and blood, gold, white.
Vision 4 (chapters 22-24) is short. It is 'a figure of the suffering that is coming' (22:1).
readings: The beast is a picture of a persecution Hermas expected soon. Faith and a single mind carry the believer through it unharmed in spirit.
The four colors (24:2-5) run from this world to its destruction by fire and blood to the age to come: the beast is the last great suffering before the end.

views.N: The beast from the sea (Revelation 13:1), the fiery locusts (Revelation 9:3), and Daniel's beasts (Daniel 7:3) stand behind the vision; faith 'put on' is Paul's armor (1 Thessalonians 5:8; Ephesians 6:16).
views.J: A sea monster is the old chaos beast of the Hebrew Bible, Leviathan (Job 41; Isaiah 27:1); Lake translates 'some Leviathan'.
views.R: Hermas gives a real-sounding route: a place about ten stades off the main road, reached by the Campanian Way. The vision comes in the middle of ordinary life outside Rome.

echoes: Revelation 13:1-2; Revelation 9:3; Daniel 7:3; Job 41:1; Isaiah 27:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Ephesians 6:16; Joel 2:1-11

settings.what: The voice like an echo
settings.by: A voice, with no speaker seen
settings.to: Hermas, praying as he walked
settings.when: On the Campanian Way, just before the beast appears
settings.why: To arm Hermas in advance with one word, 'Do not be double-minded', which he remembers when the beast comes (22:7).
settings.readers: Believers facing a coming persecution, for whom the one word was the whole defense.

title: Vision 4.2: The young woman in white and the angel Thegri
sum: Thirty feet past the beast, a young woman meets Hermas, dressed all in white as if coming from a bridal room, veiled to her forehead, with white hair. He knows she is the Church. Did nothing meet you? 'Such a beast! It could destroy whole peoples.' She tells him he escaped because he threw his worry on God and believed he could be saved through nothing but the great and glorious Name. The Lord sent his angel over the beasts, Thegri, to shut its mouth. He must tell the chosen that the beast is a figure of the great suffering to come: if they repent with all their heart and serve the Lord blamelessly, they can escape it. Woe to those who hear and refuse.

views.N: The angel shutting the beast's mouth is Daniel 6:22; salvation through no other name is Acts 4:12; 'better not to be born' is Matthew 26:24. The bride recalls Revelation 21:2.
views.J: Lake: 'No other mention of this Angel is found in Jewish or Christian literature'; he reports Rendel Harris's proposal to read Segri, from Hebrew sagar, 'to shut' (Daniel 6:22). Angels set over parts of creation are a Jewish idea (1 Enoch 20).
views.D: The way through persecution is faith in the Name and a single mind; the book's word for the opposite, 'double-minded', returns in 23:6.

echoes: Daniel 6:22; Hebrews 11:33; Acts 4:12; Psalm 55:22; 1 Peter 5:7; Matthew 26:24; Mark 14:21; Psalm 19:5; Revelation 21:2

settings.what: The Church's explanation of the beast
settings.by: The Church, as a young woman in white
settings.to: Hermas, just past the beast; through him 'the Lord's chosen' (23:5)
settings.when: On the road, moments after he passed the beast
settings.why: To turn Hermas's escape into a message for the church: faith and repentance carry believers through the coming persecution, and refusal brings woe.
settings.readers: Roman believers bracing for persecution, who needed courage and a reason not to deny.

title: Vision 4.3: The four colors
sum: Curious again, Hermas asks about the beast's colors. Black is this world. Fire and blood mean this world must be destroyed by blood and fire. Gold is the believers who have escaped this world: tested by fire as gold is, those who hold out will be cleansed and made useful for the tower. White is the age to come, where God's chosen will live, spotless and pure. Hermas must keep speaking into the saints' ears; if they are willing, the coming suffering 'will be nothing'. Then a cloud comes, she is gone, and Hermas turns in fear, thinking the beast is coming back.
The Visions of the Church end here. In Vision 5 (25) the Shepherd appears, and the Mandates begin.

views.N: Gold tested by fire is 1 Peter 1:7; the world ending in fire is 2 Peter 3:7, 10. The four colors may be compared with Revelation's four horses (Revelation 6:1-8), though the meanings differ.
views.J: Gold refined in the furnace is Jewish wisdom (Proverbs 17:3; Sirach 2:5).
views.D: 'If you are willing, it will be nothing': the book holds that the believers' repentance shapes how they meet the end, whether the suffering is averted or only made harmless.

echoes: 1 Peter 1:7; 1 Peter 4:12; 2 Peter 3:7; 2 Peter 3:10; Joel 2:30; Proverbs 17:3; Sirach 2:5; Revelation 6:1-8; Malachi 3:2-3

settings.what: The meaning of the four colors
settings.by: The Church, as a young woman
settings.to: Hermas, to speak to 'the saints'
settings.when: At the end of the fourth vision
settings.why: To give the believers a map of the end and a place in it: they are the gold, tested now, bound for the white age to come.
settings.readers: The saints in Rome, into whose ears Hermas is to keep speaking (24:6), told that they are the gold being tested now.
